original.title: A rational integrating factor
original.stem_html:
A differentiable function satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{2 x + 8}{x^{2} + 8 x + 12}\,y=6\]

and \(y(0)=2\).
original.question_html:
A differentiable function satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{2 x + 8}{x^{2} + 8 x + 12}\,y=6\]

and \(y(0)=2\).

(a)[8]

Find the particular solution in exact logarithmic form.

(b)[1]

State the maximal open interval containing \(x=0\) on which the equation and this solution are defined.
original.hint_html:
(a)

The numerator of the coefficient of \(y\) is the derivative of the quadratic denominator.

(b)

Do not cross a zero of the coefficient denominator.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\left(\frac{3 \ln{\left(\frac{3 x + 6}{x + 6} \right)}}{2} + \frac{1}{6}\right) \left(x^{2} + 8 x + 12\right)\]

(b)

\[x\gt -2.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{2 x + 8}{x^{2} + 8 x + 12}\,y=6\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{- 2 x - 8}{x^{2} + 8 x + 12}\,\mathrm d x\right)=\frac{1}{x^{2} + 8 x + 12}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=\frac{6}{x^{2} + 8 x + 12}.\]

Factor the quadratic and use partial fractions:

\[\frac6{(x+2)(x+6)}=\frac{3}{2(x+2)}-\frac{3}{2(x+6)}.\]
\[\mu y=\frac{3 \ln{\left(\frac{x + 2}{x + 6} \right)}}{2}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[\frac{1}{6}=- \frac{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}+C,\qquad C=\frac{1}{6} + \frac{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}.\]

Therefore

\[y=\left(x^{2} + 8 x + 12\right) \left(\frac{3 \ln{\left(\frac{x + 2}{x + 6} \right)}}{2} + \frac{1}{6} + \frac{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}\right).\]

On the interval containing the initial point the logarithms combine to give

\[y=\left(\frac{3 \ln{\left(\frac{3 x + 6}{x + 6} \right)}}{2} + \frac{1}{6}\right) \left(x^{2} + 8 x + 12\right).\]

(b)

The coefficient is undefined at \(x=-6,-2\). The connected interval containing zero is \((-2,\infty)\); there the logarithm argument is positive.

original.title: Completing the square inside an integrating factor
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{x - 2}{x^{2} - 4 x + 13}\,y=2\]

with \(y(6)=5\).
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{x - 2}{x^{2} - 4 x + 13}\,y=2\]

with \(y(6)=5\).

(a)[9]

Find \(y\) in exact logarithmic form.

(b)[1]

Explain why the formula is real for every real \(x\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use \((x-2)^2+3^2\) and an integrating factor proportional to its reciprocal square root.

(b)

Compare the square root with \(|x-2|\).
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9} \left(2 \ln{\left(\frac{x}{9} + \frac{\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9}}{9} - \frac{2}{9} \right)} + 1\right)\]

(b)

The square root is always positive and \(x-2+\sqrt{(x-2)^2+9}\gt 0\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{x - 2}{x^{2} - 4 x + 13}\,y=2\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{2 - x}{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9}\,\mathrm d x\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9}}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9}}.\]

Complete the square and use the inverse hyperbolic sine integral:

\[\int\frac{2}{\sqrt{(x-2)^2+9}}\,\mathrm dx=2\sinh^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x-2}{3}\right).\]
\[\mu y=2 \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{3} - \frac{2}{3} \right)}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[1=2 \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{3} \right)}+C,\qquad C=1 - 2 \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{3} \right)}.\]

Therefore

\[y=\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9} \left(2 \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{3} - \frac{2}{3} \right)} - 2 \sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{3} \right)} + 1\right).\]

Since \(\sinh^{-1}(4/3)=\ln3\), use the logarithmic form of inverse hyperbolic sine:

\[y=\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9} \left(2 \ln{\left(\frac{x}{9} + \frac{\sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9}}{9} - \frac{2}{9} \right)} + 1\right).\]

(b)

Because \(\sqrt{(x-2)^2+9}\gt |x-2|\), the numerator inside the logarithm is strictly positive, even when \(x\lt 2\).

original.title: Choosing the other radical factor
original.stem_html:
Consider the equation

\[\sqrt{x^{2} + 9}\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -y=x \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}\]

with \(y(4)=2\).
original.question_html:
Consider the equation

\[\sqrt{x^{2} + 9}\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -y=x \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}\]

with \(y(4)=2\).

(a)[3]

Show that \(\sqrt{x^2+9}-x\) is an integrating factor after the equation has been put in linear form.

(b)[6]

Hence find the particular solution.

(c)[1]

Explain why division by this integrating factor is valid for all real \(x\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

It is enough to check \(\mu^\prime=P\mu\).

(b)

Integrate \(x\sqrt{x^2+9}-x^2\) before applying \(x=4\).

(c)

Use the positive square root.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\mu=\sqrt{x^2+9}-x.\]

(b)

\[y=\frac{- \frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{\left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - \frac{55}{3}}{- x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}}\]

(c)

\(\mu\gt 0\) for every real \(x\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Dividing by the square root gives \(P(x)=-1/\sqrt{x^2+9}\). If \(\mu=\sqrt{x^2+9}-x\), then

\[\mu^\prime=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+9}}-1=-\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{x^2+9}}.\]

Thus \(\mu^\prime/\mu=P\), as required.

(b)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 9}}\,y=x\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int - \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 9}}\,\mathrm d x\right)=- x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=x \left(- x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}\right).\]

After multiplication the right side is \(x\sqrt{x^2+9}-x^2\). Use \(u=x^2+9\) for the radical term.

\[\mu y=- \frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{\left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[2=\frac{61}{3}+C,\qquad C=- \frac{55}{3}.\]

Therefore

\[y=\frac{- \frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{\left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - \frac{55}{3}}{- x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 9}}.\]

(c)

\(\sqrt{x^2+9}\gt |x|\), so \(\sqrt{x^2+9}-x\gt 0\).

original.title: A periodic input with a decaying response
original.stem_html:
Solve the initial-value problem

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +2\,y=- \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 3 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\]
\[y(0)=2.\]
original.question_html:
Solve the initial-value problem

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +2\,y=- \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 3 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\]
\[y(0)=2.\]
(a)[7]

Use an integrating factor to find \(y\) explicitly.

(b)[2]

Does \(y\) tend to a finite limit as \(x\to\infty\)? Justify your answer.
original.hint_html:
(a)

The antiderivative of \(e^{2x}(3\cos2x-\sin2x)\) has the form \(e^{2x}(a\cos2x+b\sin2x)\).

(b)

Decay of the transient term does not make a nonconstant periodic term converge.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\frac{\sin{\left(2 x \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 x \right)} + e^{- 2 x}\]

(b)

No. It approaches a periodic function, not a constant.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +2\,y=- \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 3 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int 2\,\mathrm d x\right)=e^{2 x}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=\left(- \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 3 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\right) e^{2 x}.\]

Integrate the exponential–trigonometric expression by parts twice, or differentiate the proposed antiderivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left[e^{2x}\left(\cos2x+\tfrac12\sin2x\right)\right]=e^{2x}(3\cos2x-\sin2x).\]
\[\mu y=\left(\frac{\sin{\left(2 x \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\right) e^{2 x}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[2=1+C,\qquad C=1.\]

Therefore

\[y=\left(\left(\frac{\sin{\left(2 x \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\right) e^{2 x} + 1\right) e^{- 2 x}.\]

(b)

The exponential term tends to zero. At \(x=n\pi\) the limiting values are \(1\), whereas at \(x=n\pi+\pi/2\) they are \(-1\). Hence a single limit does not exist.

original.title: Two partial-fraction steps
original.stem_html:
For \(x\gt 0\),

\[\left(x^{2} + 4 x\right)\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +4\,y=2 x\]

and \(y(2)=1\).
original.question_html:
For \(x\gt 0\),

\[\left(x^{2} + 4 x\right)\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +4\,y=2 x\]

and \(y(2)=1\).

(a)[9]

Find the particular solution in the form \(y=f(x)\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use partial fractions both for the integrating factor and for the resulting integral.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=-1 + \frac{\left(2 x + 8\right) \ln{\left(\frac{x}{6} + \frac{2}{3} \right)}}{x} + \frac{4}{x}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\frac{4}{x^{2} + 4 x}\,y=\frac{2}{x + 4}\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{4}{x \left(x + 4\right)}\,\mathrm d x\right)=\frac{x}{x + 4}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=\frac{2 x}{\left(x + 4\right)^{2}}.\]

Use

\[\frac4{x(x+4)}=\frac1x-\frac1{x+4},\qquad \frac{2x}{(x+4)^2}=\frac2{x+4}-\frac8{(x+4)^2}.\]
\[\mu y=2 \ln{\left(x + 4 \right)} + \frac{8}{x + 4}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[\frac{1}{3}=\frac{4}{3} + \ln{\left(36 \right)}+C,\qquad C=- \ln{\left(36 \right)} - 1.\]

Therefore

\[y=\frac{\left(x + 4\right) \left(2 \ln{\left(x + 4 \right)} - \ln{\left(36 \right)} - 1 + \frac{8}{x + 4}\right)}{x}.\]

An equivalent simplified form is

\[y=-1 + \frac{\left(2 x + 8\right) \ln{\left(\frac{x}{6} + \frac{2}{3} \right)}}{x} + \frac{4}{x}.\]

original.title: A time-dependent rational coefficient
original.stem_html:
For \(t\gt 2/3\), the function \(x(t)\) satisfies

\[\left(9 t^{2} - 4\right)\,\frac{\mathrm d x}{\mathrm d t} +12\,x=18 t^{2} - 8\]

and \(x(1)=5\).
original.question_html:
For \(t\gt 2/3\), the function \(x(t)\) satisfies

\[\left(9 t^{2} - 4\right)\,\frac{\mathrm d x}{\mathrm d t} +12\,x=18 t^{2} - 8\]

and \(x(1)=5\).

(a)[9]

Find \(x\) as an exact function of \(t\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Keep the factor 3 when integrating \((3t\pm2)^{-1}\).
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[x=\frac{\left(3 t + 2\right) \left(2 t + \frac{8 \ln{\left(\frac{5}{3 t + 2} \right)}}{3} - 1\right)}{3 t - 2}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d x}{\mathrm d t} +\frac{12}{9 t^{2} - 4}\,x=2\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(t)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{12}{9 t^{2} - 4}\,\mathrm d t\right)=\frac{3 t - 2}{3 t + 2}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d t}\left(\mu x\right)=\frac{2 \left(3 t - 2\right)}{3 t + 2}.\]

The coefficient splits as

\[\frac{12}{9t^2-4}=\frac3{3t-2}-\frac3{3t+2}.\]

For the final integral use \(2(3t-2)/(3t+2)=2-8/(3t+2)\).

\[\mu x=2 t - \frac{8 \ln{\left(3 t + 2 \right)}}{3}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[1=2 - \frac{8 \ln{\left(5 \right)}}{3}+C,\qquad C=-1 + \frac{8 \ln{\left(5 \right)}}{3}.\]

Therefore

\[x=\frac{\left(3 t + 2\right) \left(2 t - \frac{8 \ln{\left(3 t + 2 \right)}}{3} - 1 + \frac{8 \ln{\left(5 \right)}}{3}\right)}{3 t - 2}.\]
\[x=\frac{\left(3 t + 2\right) \left(2 t + \frac{8 \ln{\left(\frac{5}{3 t + 2} \right)}}{3} - 1\right)}{3 t - 2}.\]

original.title: A half-angle factor and a minimum
original.stem_html:
For \(0\lt \theta\lt \pi\),

\[\sin{\left(\theta \right)}\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d \theta} +y=3 \tan{\left(\frac{\theta}{2} \right)}\]

and \(y(\pi/2)=2\).
original.question_html:
For \(0\lt \theta\lt \pi\),

\[\sin{\left(\theta \right)}\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d \theta} +y=3 \tan{\left(\frac{\theta}{2} \right)}\]

and \(y(\pi/2)=2\).

(a)[7]

Find the particular solution.

(b)[2]

Find the minimum value of \(y\) and the value of \(\theta\) where it occurs.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(\int\operatorname{cosec}\theta\,d\theta=\ln\tan(\theta/2)\) on this interval.

(b)

Minimise as a function of the positive half-angle tangent.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\frac{3 \tan{\left(\frac{\theta}{2} \right)}}{2} + \frac{1}{2 \tan{\left(\frac{\theta}{2} \right)}}\]

(b)

\[y_{\min}=\sqrt3,\qquad \theta=\frac\pi3.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Divide by \(\sin\theta\). Since \(0\lt \theta\lt \pi\), an integrating factor is

\[\mu=\exp\!\left(\int\operatorname{cosec}\theta\,\mathrm d\theta\right)=\tan\frac\theta2.\]
\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\theta}\left(y\tan\frac\theta2\right)=\frac32\tan\frac\theta2\sec^2\frac\theta2.\]

Put \(u=\tan(\theta/2)\). Then \(du=\tfrac12\sec^2(\theta/2)\,d\theta\), so the integral is \(\tfrac32u^2\).

\[y\tan\frac\theta2=\frac32\tan^2\frac\theta2+C.\]

The condition \(y(\pi/2)=2\) gives \(C=1/2\).

\[y=\frac{3 \tan{\left(\frac{\theta}{2} \right)}}{2} + \frac{1}{2 \tan{\left(\frac{\theta}{2} \right)}}.\]

(b)

Put \(u=\tan(\theta/2)\gt 0\). Then \(y=3u/2+1/(2u)\). Differentiating with respect to \(u\) gives \(3/2-1/(2u^2)=0\), hence \(u=1/\sqrt3\). The expression tends to infinity at both ends and has positive second derivative \(u^{-3}\). Thus the unique minimum is \(\sqrt3\) at \(\theta=\pi/3\).

original.title: Conjugate radicals and a finite limit
original.stem_html:
For \(x\gt 2\),

\[\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +y=x \left(x - \sqrt{x^{2} - 4}\right)\]

and \(y(5/2)=2\).
original.question_html:
For \(x\gt 2\),

\[\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +y=x \left(x - \sqrt{x^{2} - 4}\right)\]

and \(y(5/2)=2\).

(a)[3]

Show that \(x+\sqrt{x^2-4}\) is an integrating factor in standard linear form.

(b)[6]

Hence find \(y\) explicitly.

(c)[2]

Find \(\lim_{x\to\infty}y\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Check the logarithmic derivative of the proposed factor.

(b)

Multiply the conjugate radical factors before integrating.

(c)

Do not drop the square-root term from the denominator.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\mu=x+\sqrt{x^2-4}.\]

(b)

\[y=\frac{4 \sqrt{x^{2} - 4} + 2}{x + \sqrt{x^{2} - 4}}\]

(c)

\[\lim_{x\to\infty}y=2.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

After dividing by \(r=\sqrt{x^2-4}\), the coefficient is \(1/r\). Also \(\mu^\prime=1+x/r=(x+r)/r=\mu/r\).

(b)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}}\,y=\frac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}} - x\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}}\,\mathrm d x\right)=x + \sqrt{x^{2} - 4}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=\frac{4 x}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}}.\]

The key simplification is \((x+r)(x-r)=4\), where \(r=\sqrt{x^2-4}\). Therefore the multiplied right side is \(4x/r\).

\[\mu y=4 \sqrt{x^{2} - 4}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[8=6+C,\qquad C=2.\]

Therefore

\[y=\frac{4 \sqrt{x^{2} - 4} + 2}{x + \sqrt{x^{2} - 4}}.\]

(c)

Divide numerator and denominator of \(y=(4r+2)/(x+r)\) by \(x\). Since \(r/x\to1\), the limit is \(4/(1+1)=2\).

original.title: An exponential that matches the complementary function
original.stem_html:
The initial-value problem is

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +3\,y=2 e^{- 3 x}\]
\[y(0)=-1.\]
original.question_html:
The initial-value problem is

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +3\,y=2 e^{- 3 x}\]
\[y(0)=-1.\]
(a)[5]

Find the particular solution.

(b)[1]

Find the point where the solution crosses the \(x\)-axis.
original.hint_html:
(a)

After multiplication by \(e^{3x}\) the right side becomes constant.

(b)

Only the linear factor can vanish.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\left(2 x - 1\right) e^{- 3 x}\]

(b)

\[(x,y)=\left(\frac12,0\right).\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +3\,y=2 e^{- 3 x}\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int 3\,\mathrm d x\right)=e^{3 x}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=2.\]
\[\mu y=2 x+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[-1=0+C,\qquad C=-1.\]

Therefore

\[y=\left(2 x - 1\right) e^{- 3 x}.\]

(b)

The exponential factor is never zero, so \(2x-1=0\).

original.title: A radical factor with two zero crossings
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\left(x^{2} + 4\right)\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\sqrt{x^{2} + 4}\,y=x \left(x - \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}\right)\]

with \(y(0)=\ln3\).
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\left(x^{2} + 4\right)\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\sqrt{x^{2} + 4}\,y=x \left(x - \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}\right)\]

with \(y(0)=\ln3\).

(a)[4]

Show that \(x+\sqrt{x^2+4}\) is an integrating factor in linear form.

(b)[5]

Find the particular solution.

(c)[2]

Find all real zeros of the solution.
original.hint_html:
(a)

A nonzero constant multiple of an integrating factor is equally valid.

(b)

Use the product of the two conjugate radical factors.

(c)

A zero logarithm has argument 1, not 0.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\mu=x+\sqrt{x^2+4}.\]

(b)

\[y=\frac{2 \ln{\left(\frac{12}{x^{2} + 4} \right)}}{x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}}\]

(c)

\[x=\pm2\sqrt2.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The standard coefficient is \(P=(x^2+4)^{-1/2}\). Hence \(\int P\,dx=\sinh^{-1}(x/2)\). Exponentiation gives \((x+\sqrt{x^2+4})/2\); multiplying by 2 produces the stated factor.

(b)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 4}}\,y=\frac{x \left(x - \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}\right)}{x^{2} + 4}\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 4}}\,\mathrm d x\right)=x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=- \frac{4 x}{x^{2} + 4}.\]

Use \((x+r)(x-r)=-4\). The multiplied right side simplifies to \(-4x/(x^2+4)\), whose integral is \(-2\ln(x^2+4)\).

\[\mu y=- 2 \ln{\left(x^{2} + 4 \right)}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[\ln{\left(9 \right)}=- \ln{\left(16 \right)}+C,\qquad C=\ln{\left(144 \right)}.\]

Therefore

\[y=\frac{- 2 \ln{\left(x^{2} + 4 \right)} + \ln{\left(144 \right)}}{x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}}.\]

Combine the logarithms to obtain

\[y=\frac{2 \ln{\left(\frac{12}{x^{2} + 4} \right)}}{x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}}.\]

(c)

The denominator is positive for every real \(x\). Thus \(\ln(12/(x^2+4))=0\), giving \(x^2+4=12\). Both real signs are admissible.

original.title: A scaled hyperbolic integrating factor
original.stem_html: Use exponential definitions where requested.
original.question_html:
Use exponential definitions where requested.

(a)[3]

Prove \(2\sinh^2(2x)=\cosh(4x)-1\) from the exponential definitions.

(b)[7]

Solve

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +2 \coth{\left(2 x \right)}\,y=6 \sinh{\left(2 x \right)}\]

for \(x\gt 0\), given that \(y=1\) when \(x=\tfrac12\ln3\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the square; the middle term is \(-2\).

(b)

Take \(\mu=\sinh2x\) and use part (a) for the resulting integral.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[2\sinh^2(2x)=\cosh4x-1.\]

(b)

\[y=\frac{- 3 x + \frac{3 \sinh{\left(4 x \right)}}{4} - 2 + \frac{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}}{\sinh{\left(2 x \right)}}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[2\left(\frac{e^{2x}-e^{-2x}}2\right)^2=\frac{e^{4x}+e^{-4x}-2}2=\cosh4x-1.\]

(b)

The integrating factor on \(x\gt 0\) is \(\sinh2x\), since its logarithmic derivative is \(2\coth2x\).

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(y\sinh2x)=6\sinh^2 2x=3(\cosh4x-1).\]
\[y\sinh2x=\frac34\sinh4x-3x+C.\]

At \(x=\tfrac12\ln3\), \(\sinh2x=4/3\) and \(\sinh4x=40/9\). Thus

\[\frac43=\frac{10}3-\frac32\ln3+C,\qquad C=\frac32\ln3-2.\]
\[y=\frac{- 3 x + \frac{3 \sinh{\left(4 x \right)}}{4} - 2 + \frac{3 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2}}{\sinh{\left(2 x \right)}}.\]

original.title: A polynomial times an exponential
original.stem_html:
For \(x\gt 0\),

\[x\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +2\,y=x e^{2 x}\]

and \(y(1)=1\).
original.question_html:
For \(x\gt 0\),

\[x\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +2\,y=x e^{2 x}\]

and \(y(1)=1\).

(a)[7]

Find the particular solution.

(b)[1]

Find \(\lim_{x\to\infty}y e^{-2x}\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

After using \(\mu=x^2\), integrate \(x^2e^{2x}\) by parts twice.

(b)

Simplify the ratio rather than trying to subtract two divergent expressions.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\frac{\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{4}\right) e^{2 x} - \frac{e^{2}}{4} + 1}{x^{2}}\]

(b)

\[\lim_{x\to\infty}y e^{-2x}=\frac12.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\frac{2}{x}\,y=e^{2 x}\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{2}{x}\,\mathrm d x\right)=x^{2}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=x^{2} e^{2 x}.\]

Two integrations by parts give

\[\int x^2e^{2x}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{x^2e^{2x}}2-\int xe^{2x}\,\mathrm dx=e^{2x}\left(\frac{x^2}2-\frac x2+\frac14\right).\]
\[\mu y=\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{4}\right) e^{2 x}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[1=\frac{e^{2}}{4}+C,\qquad C=1 - \frac{e^{2}}{4}.\]

Therefore

\[y=\frac{\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{4}\right) e^{2 x} - \frac{e^{2}}{4} + 1}{x^{2}}.\]

(b)

Divide the explicit expression by \(e^{2x}\). The remaining nonconstant terms are multiples of \(x^{-1},x^{-2},x^{-2}e^{-2x}\), all of which tend to zero.

original.title: A positive polynomial integrating factor
original.stem_html:
Find the solution of

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\frac{6 x}{3 x^{2} + 2}\,y=x^{2}\]

that satisfies \(y(0)=3\).
original.question_html:
Find the solution of

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\frac{6 x}{3 x^{2} + 2}\,y=x^{2}\]

that satisfies \(y(0)=3\).

(a)[7]

Give your answer as a single rational expression in \(x\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Recognise \(6x/(3x^2+2)\) as a logarithmic derivative.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\frac{9 x^{5} + 10 x^{3} + 90}{15 \left(3 x^{2} + 2\right)}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} +\frac{6 x}{3 x^{2} + 2}\,y=x^{2}\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int \frac{6 x}{3 x^{2} + 2}\,\mathrm d x\right)=3 x^{2} + 2.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=x^{2} \left(3 x^{2} + 2\right).\]

The multiplied right side is \(3x^4+2x^2\), so integrate term by term.

\[\mu y=\frac{3 x^{5}}{5} + \frac{2 x^{3}}{3}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[6=0+C,\qquad C=6.\]

Therefore

\[y=\frac{\frac{3 x^{5}}{5} + \frac{2 x^{3}}{3} + 6}{3 x^{2} + 2}.\]

original.title: Integrating an inverse sine inside a linear equation
original.stem_html: Use \(0\lt x\lt 4\) throughout.
original.question_html:
Use \(0\lt x\lt 4\) throughout.

(a)[3]

Use \(u=4-(x-2)^2\) to find \(\int (x-2)/\sqrt{4-(x-2)^2}\,dx\).

(b)[9]

Find the solution of

\[xy^\prime-y=x^2\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x-2}{2}\right)\]

with \(y(2)=3\).

(c)[2]

Find \(\lim_{x\to4^-}y\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Keep the negative sign from the substitution.

(b)

An integrating factor is \(1/x\). Use integration by parts and then part (a).

(c)

Use the branch \(-\pi/2\le\sin^{-1}u\le\pi/2\).
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\int\frac{x-2}{\sqrt{4-(x-2)^2}}\,\mathrm dx=-\sqrt{4-(x-2)^2}+C.\]

(b)

\[y=x \left(\sqrt{4 - \left(x - 2\right)^{2}} + \left(x - 2\right) \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} - 1 \right)} - \frac{1}{2}\right)\]

(c)

\[\lim_{x\to4^-}y=4\pi-2.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The substitution gives \(du=-2(x-2)dx\). The integral becomes \(-\tfrac12\int u^{-1/2}du=-\sqrt u+C\). Substitute back.

(b)

Put the equation in first-order linear form:

\[\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d x} -\frac{1}{x}\,y=x \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} - 1 \right)}\]

An integrating factor is

\[\mu(x)=\exp\!\left(\int - \frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm d x\right)=\frac{1}{x}.\]

Multiplication by the integrating factor makes the left side a product derivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d x}\left(\mu y\right)=\sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} - 1 \right)}.\]

Integration by parts, with \(w=\sin^{-1}((x-2)/2)\) and \(dv=dx\), is most conveniently written using the shifted factor \(x-2\):

\[\int\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x-2}{2}\right)\,\mathrm dx=(x-2)\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x-2}{2}\right)-\int\frac{x-2}{\sqrt{4-(x-2)^2}}\,\mathrm dx.\]
\[\mu y=\sqrt{4 - \left(x - 2\right)^{2}} + \left(x - 2\right) \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} - 1 \right)}+C.\]

Apply the initial condition before dividing by the integrating factor:

\[\frac{3}{2}=2+C,\qquad C=- \frac{1}{2}.\]

Therefore

\[y=x \left(\sqrt{4 - \left(x - 2\right)^{2}} + \left(x - 2\right) \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} - 1 \right)} - \frac{1}{2}\right).\]

original.title: Salt concentration in a well-mixed tank
original.stem_html: A tank contains 30 litres of liquid and initially no salt. Brine containing 3 grams of salt per litre enters at 2 litres per minute. The well-mixed liquid leaves at the same rate. Let \(S(t)\) be the mass of salt, in grams, after \(t\) minutes. Assume constant flow rates and instantaneous mixing.
original.question_html:
A tank contains 30 litres of liquid and initially no salt. Brine containing 3 grams of salt per litre enters at 2 litres per minute. The well-mixed liquid leaves at the same rate. Let \(S(t)\) be the mass of salt, in grams, after \(t\) minutes. Assume constant flow rates and instantaneous mixing.

(a)[2]

Form a differential equation for \(S\).

(b)[5]

Solve the equation and give the concentration as a function of \(t\).

(c)[2]

Find the first time at which the concentration reaches 2 grams per litre.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use mass rate in minus mass rate out, not concentration rate directly.

(b)

The mass and the concentration differ by the fixed factor 30.

(c)

Use the concentration formula, not \(S=2\).
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{\mathrm dS}{\mathrm dt}=6-\frac{S}{15},\qquad S(0)=0.\]

(b)

\[S=90(1-e^{-t/15}),\qquad c=3(1-e^{-t/15})\ \mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}.\]

(c)

\[t=15\ln3\ \text{minutes}.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The inflow adds \(2\times3=6\) grams per minute. The concentration inside the tank is \(S/30\) grams per litre, so the outflow removes \(2S/30=S/15\) grams per minute. Subtract removal from input.

(b)

The integrating factor is \(e^{t/15}\).

\[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(Se^{t/15})=6e^{t/15},\qquad Se^{t/15}=90e^{t/15}+C.\]

Since \(S(0)=0\), \(C=-90\). Divide by \(e^{t/15}\) and then by the tank volume 30 to obtain the concentration.

(c)

\(3(1-e^{-t/15})=2\) gives \(e^{-t/15}=1/3\). The concentration is strictly increasing for \(t\ge0\), so this is the unique first crossing.

original.title: An exceptional value of a parameter
original.stem_html:
For a real constant \(k\),

\[y^\prime+ky=4e^{-2x},\qquad y(0)=1.\]
original.question_html:
For a real constant \(k\),

\[y^\prime+ky=4e^{-2x},\qquad y(0)=1.\]
(a)[4]

Find the solution when \(k\ne2\).

(b)[3]

Find the solution when \(k=2\).

(c)[1]

State the limiting value of \(y\) as \(x\to\infty\) when \(k\gt 0\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Keep the factor \(k-2\) in the antiderivative.

(b)

Solve the exceptional equation separately.

(c)

Include the exceptional parameter case in the conclusion.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\frac{\left(k - 6\right) e^{- k x}}{k - 2} + \frac{4 e^{- 2 x}}{k - 2}\]

(b)

\[y=(1+4x)e^{-2x}.\]

(c)

\[y\longrightarrow0\quad(k\gt 0).\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The integrating factor is \(e^{kx}\). For \(k\ne2\),

\[ye^{kx}=\frac4{k-2}e^{(k-2)x}+C.\]

The initial condition gives \(C=1-4/(k-2)=(k-6)/(k-2)\).

\[y=\frac{\left(k - 6\right) e^{- k x}}{k - 2} + \frac{4 e^{- 2 x}}{k - 2}.\]

(b)

Now the multiplied equation is \((ye^{2x})^\prime=4\). Thus \(ye^{2x}=4x+C\) and \(C=1\). The formula from part (a) must not be used by direct substitution into its zero denominator.

(c)

For \(k\ne2\) both exponential terms decay. For \(k=2\), the polynomial-times-decaying-exponential term also tends to zero.

original.title: Inferring an equilibrium level from three observations
original.stem_html:
A measured response \(T(t)\) follows the model

\[\frac{\mathrm dT}{\mathrm dt}=-k(T-A),\qquad k\gt 0,\]

where \(A\) and \(k\) are constants. Exact observations are \(T(0)=20\), \(T(2)=12\) and \(T(4)=8\).
original.question_html:
A measured response \(T(t)\) follows the model

\[\frac{\mathrm dT}{\mathrm dt}=-k(T-A),\qquad k\gt 0,\]

where \(A\) and \(k\) are constants. Exact observations are \(T(0)=20\), \(T(2)=12\) and \(T(4)=8\).

(a)[3]

Solve the equation in terms of \(A\) and \(k\), using \(T(0)=20\).

(b)[3]

Use the other two observations to determine \(A\) and \(k\).

(c)[2]

Find the first time when \(T=6\) and state the limiting response.
original.hint_html:
(a)

The equilibrium level is \(A\), not zero.

(b)

The decreases over equal time intervals form a geometric sequence.

(c)

Use the solved model to check the interpretation of both parameters.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[T=A+(20-A)e^{-kt}.\]

(b)

\[A=4,\qquad k=\frac12\ln2.\]

(c)

\[t=6,\qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}T=4.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Put the equation in the form \(T^\prime+kT=kA\). The integrating factor is \(e^{kt}\), so \((Te^{kt})^\prime=kAe^{kt}\). Integration gives \(T=A+Ce^{-kt}\); the first observation gives \(C=20-A\).

(b)

Let \(q=e^{-2k}\), so \(0\lt q\lt 1\). The consecutive decreases are \(20-12=8\) and \(12-8=4\). In this exponential model their ratio is \(q\), hence \(q=1/2\). Then \(12=A+(20-A)/2\) gives \(A=4\) and \(e^{-2k}=1/2\) gives \(k=\tfrac12\ln2\).

(c)

Now \(T=4+16\,2^{-t/2}\). Setting \(T=6\) gives \(2^{-t/2}=1/8=2^{-3}\), hence \(t=6\). The exponential term decays, so the limit is 4. Since the solution decreases strictly from 20, the crossing is unique.

original.title: Three root types in one homogeneous family
original.stem_html:
For \(t\ge0\), consider

\[y^{\prime\prime}+2ky^\prime+9y=0.\]
original.question_html:
For \(t\ge0\), consider

\[y^{\prime\prime}+2ky^\prime+9y=0.\]
(a)[2]

Find the general solution when \(k=0\).

(b)[2]

Find the general solution when \(k=3\).

(c)[2]

Find the general solution when \(k=5\).

(d)[2]

For which of the three values of \(k\) does every solution tend to zero as \(t\to\infty\)? Explain.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation for this value of \(k\).

(b)

Solve the auxiliary equation for this value of \(k\).

(c)

Solve the auxiliary equation for this value of \(k\).

(d)

The word “every” rules out merely finding one solution with a zero limit.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=C_{1} \cos{\left(3 t \right)} + C_{2} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}\]

(b)

\[y=\left(C_{1} + C_{2} t\right) e^{- 3 t}\]

(c)

\[y=C_{1} e^{- t} + C_{2} e^{- 9 t}\]

(d)

\(k=3\) and \(k=5\) only.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation is \(m^2+9=0\), with roots \(\pm3i\).

\[y=C_{1} \cos{\left(3 t \right)} + C_{2} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}\]

(b)

The auxiliary equation is \((m+3)^2=0\), so the repeated root requires the factor \(C_1+C_2t\).

\[y=\left(C_{1} + C_{2} t\right) e^{- 3 t}\]

(c)

The auxiliary equation is \((m+1)(m+9)=0\), with two distinct negative real roots.

\[y=C_{1} e^{- t} + C_{2} e^{- 9 t}\]

(d)

At \(k=3\) and \(k=5\) every complementary term decays. At \(k=0\) a nonzero sine/cosine combination continues to oscillate; only the zero solution tends to zero.

original.title: The first zero of a damped homogeneous solution
original.stem_html:
For \(t\ge0\),

\[y^{\prime\prime}+4y^\prime+13y=0,\qquad y(0)=2,\quad y^\prime(0)=-1.\]
original.question_html:
For \(t\ge0\),

\[y^{\prime\prime}+4y^\prime+13y=0,\qquad y(0)=2,\quad y^\prime(0)=-1.\]
(a)[5]

Find the particular solution.

(b)[2]

Find the first positive value of \(t\) for which \(y=0\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The auxiliary roots are complex; use a real sine-and-cosine expression.

(b)

Do not use the negative principal value of the inverse tangent as the first positive time.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\left(\sin{\left(3 t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\right) e^{- 2 t}\]

(b)

\[t=- \frac{\tan^{-1}{\left(2 \right)}}{3} + \frac{\pi}{3}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation is

\[m^{2} + 4 m + 13=0,\qquad m=-2\pm 3i.\]

Use the real complementary function formed from the conjugate roots.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- 2 t} \cos{\left(3 t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)}.\]

There is no forcing term, so no nonzero particular integral is needed.

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- 3 C_{1} e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)} - 2 C_{1} e^{- 2 t} \cos{\left(3 t \right)} - 2 C_{2} e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)} + 3 C_{2} e^{- 2 t} \cos{\left(3 t \right)}.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = 2\\- 2 C_{1} + 3 C_{2} = -1\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=2,\qquad C_2=1.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(3 t \right)} + 2 e^{- 2 t} \cos{\left(3 t \right)}.\]

(b)

The exponential is nonzero, so \(2\cos3t+\sin3t=0\). The first positive solution of \(\tan3t=-2\) lies in quadrant II, giving \(3t=\pi-\tan^{-1}2\). At a zero of cosine the original expression is not zero, so no roots are lost by division.

original.title: What the arbitrary constants belong to
original.stem_html:
A general solution of

\[y^{\prime\prime}+2y^\prime+5y=10\]

is

\[y=e^{-x}(A\cos2x+B\sin2x)+2.\]
original.question_html:
A general solution of

\[y^{\prime\prime}+2y^\prime+5y=10\]

is

\[y=e^{-x}(A\cos2x+B\sin2x)+2.\]
(a)[2]

Identify the complementary function and a particular integral.

(b)[2]

Find \(A\) and \(B\) if \(y(0)=3\) and \(y^\prime(0)=0\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The particular integral need not contain an arbitrary constant.

(b)

The exponential factor contributes \(-A\) to the initial derivative.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=e^{-x}(A\cos2x+B\sin2x),\qquad y_{\mathrm{PI}}=2.\]

(b)

\[A=1,\qquad B=\frac12.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The term containing the two arbitrary constants solves the homogeneous equation. Substitution of the constant 2 gives \(5(2)=10\), so it is a particular integral.

(b)

The value condition gives \(A+2=3\), hence \(A=1\). The derivative at zero is \(-A+2B\), giving \(-1+2B=0\).

original.title: Two real modes with different long-term effects
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[6\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} -2\,y=6 t - 5\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=0\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=0\).
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[6\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} -2\,y=6 t - 5\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=0\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=0\).

(a)[8]

Find the solution satisfying these conditions, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[2]

Describe the sign and leading term of the solution for large positive \(t\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

(b)

Examine the complementary function as well as the particular integral.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=- 3 t + 2 e^{\frac{t}{2}} + 1 - 3 e^{- \frac{2 t}{3}}\]

(b)

\[y\sim2e^{t/2}\gt 0.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation has two distinct real roots:

\[\left(2 m - 1\right) \left(3 m + 2\right)=0,\qquad m=\frac{1}{2},\ - \frac{2}{3}.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{\frac{t}{2}} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{2 t}{3}}.\]

For a polynomial particular integral, try

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a_{0} + a_{1} t.\]

Substitute into the differential equation and equate coefficients of like powers:

\[\begin{aligned}- 2 a_{1} - 6 = 0\\- 2 a_{0} + a_{1} + 5 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a_{0}=1,\quad a_{1}=-3\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=1 - 3 t.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{\frac{t}{2}} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{2 t}{3}} - 3 t + 1.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=\frac{C_{1} e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2} - \frac{2 C_{2} e^{- \frac{2 t}{3}}}{3} - 3.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} + C_{2} = -1\\\frac{C_{1}}{2} - \frac{2 C_{2}}{3} = 3\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=2,\qquad C_2=-3.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=- 3 t + 2 e^{\frac{t}{2}} + 1 - 3 e^{- \frac{2 t}{3}}.\]

(b)

The term \(e^{-2t/3}\) decays and the linear term grows much more slowly than \(e^{t/2}\). The coefficient of the growing exponential is positive.

original.title: A repeated root with a quadratic input
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +4\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +4\,y=8 t^{2} + 12 t + 12\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=-1\).
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +4\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +4\,y=8 t^{2} + 12 t + 12\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=-1\).

(a)[10]

Find the solution satisfying these conditions, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=2 t^{2} - t - 4 t e^{- 2 t} + 3 - 2 e^{- 2 t}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation has a repeated real root:

\[\left(m + 2\right)^{2}=0,\qquad m=-2.\]

The repeated root requires the extra linear factor, not two copies of the same exponential.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- 2 t} + C_{2} t e^{- 2 t}.\]

For a polynomial particular integral, try

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a_{0} + a_{1} t + a_{2} t^{2}.\]

Substitute into the differential equation and equate coefficients of like powers:

\[\begin{aligned}4 a_{2} - 8 = 0\\4 a_{1} + 8 a_{2} - 12 = 0\\4 a_{0} + 4 a_{1} + 2 a_{2} - 12 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a_{0}=3,\quad a_{1}=-1,\quad a_{2}=2\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=2 t^{2} - t + 3.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 2 t} + C_{2} t e^{- 2 t} + 2 t^{2} - t + 3.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- 2 C_{1} e^{- 2 t} - 2 C_{2} t e^{- 2 t} + C_{2} e^{- 2 t} + 4 t - 1.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = -2\\- 2 C_{1} + C_{2} = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=-2,\qquad C_2=-4.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=2 t^{2} - t - 4 t e^{- 2 t} + 3 - 2 e^{- 2 t}.\]

original.title: The limiting rate of a slowly decaying response
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[100\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +20\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +y=20 t + 500\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=0\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=0\).
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[100\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +20\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +y=20 t + 500\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=0\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=0\).

(a)[10]

Find the solution satisfying these conditions, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[2]

Find \(\lim_{t\to\infty}y^\prime\) and justify why this limit does not depend on the initial conditions.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

(b)

Examine the complementary function as well as the particular integral.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=20 t - 30 t e^{- \frac{t}{10}} + 100 - 100 e^{- \frac{t}{10}}\]

(b)

\[y^\prime\longrightarrow20.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation has a repeated real root:

\[\left(10 m + 1\right)^{2}=0,\qquad m=- \frac{1}{10}.\]

The repeated root requires the extra linear factor, not two copies of the same exponential.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- \frac{t}{10}} + C_{2} t e^{- \frac{t}{10}}.\]

For a polynomial particular integral, try

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a_{0} + a_{1} t.\]

Substitute into the differential equation and equate coefficients of like powers:

\[\begin{aligned}a_{1} - 20 = 0\\a_{0} + 20 a_{1} - 500 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a_{0}=100,\quad a_{1}=20\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=20 t + 100.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- \frac{t}{10}} + C_{2} t e^{- \frac{t}{10}} + 20 t + 100.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- \frac{C_{1} e^{- \frac{t}{10}}}{10} - \frac{C_{2} t e^{- \frac{t}{10}}}{10} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{t}{10}} + 20.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = -100\\- \frac{C_{1}}{10} + C_{2} = -20\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=-100,\qquad C_2=-30.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=20 t - 30 t e^{- \frac{t}{10}} + 100 - 100 e^{- \frac{t}{10}}.\]

(b)

The derivative of \((C_1+C_2t)e^{-t/10}\) tends to zero for every fixed pair of constants. The derivative of the particular integral \(20t+100\) is 20.

original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

The function \(y\) satisfies

\[a_{0}=1,\quad a_{1}=0,\quad a_{2}=2\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- 2 C_{1} e^{- t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - C_{1} e^{- t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} - C_{2} e^{- t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 C_{2} e^{- t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + 4 t.\]

original.title: A limit valid for every initial condition
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[4\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +12\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +73\,y=219 t^{2} - t + 158\]
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[4\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +12\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +73\,y=219 t^{2} - t + 158\]
(a)[6]

Find the general solution, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[2]

Show that \(y/t^2\to3\) as \(t\to\infty\) for every choice of initial conditions.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

(b)

Examine the complementary function as well as the particular integral.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=C_{1} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \cos{\left(4 t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \sin{\left(4 t \right)} + 3 t^{2} - t + 2\]

(b)

\[\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{y}{t^2}=3.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation is

\[4 m^{2} + 12 m + 73=0,\qquad m=- \frac{3}{2}\pm 4i.\]

Use the real complementary function formed from the conjugate roots.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \cos{\left(4 t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \sin{\left(4 t \right)}.\]

For a polynomial particular integral, try

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a_{0} + a_{1} t + a_{2} t^{2}.\]

Substitute into the differential equation and equate coefficients of like powers:

\[\begin{aligned}73 a_{2} - 219 = 0\\73 a_{1} + 24 a_{2} + 1 = 0\\73 a_{0} + 12 a_{1} + 8 a_{2} - 158 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a_{0}=2,\quad a_{1}=-1,\quad a_{2}=3\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=3 t^{2} - t + 2.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \cos{\left(4 t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \sin{\left(4 t \right)} + 3 t^{2} - t + 2.\]

(b)

original.title: Choosing an initial slope that removes growth
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} -\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} -6\,y=- 6 t^{2} - 14 t + 6\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=1\).
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} -\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} -6\,y=- 6 t^{2} - 14 t + 6\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=1\).

(a)[8]

Find the solution satisfying these conditions, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[2]

Keep \(y(0)=2\) but replace the derivative condition by \(y^\prime(0)=v\). Find \(v\) for which the growing exponential term is absent.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

(b)

Remove the positive-exponent mode, not the whole complementary function.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=t^{2} + 2 t + e^{3 t} - 1 + 2 e^{- 2 t}\]

(b)

\[v=-4.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation has two distinct real roots:

\[\left(m - 3\right) \left(m + 2\right)=0,\qquad m=3,\ -2.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{3 t} + C_{2} e^{- 2 t}.\]

For a polynomial particular integral, try

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a_{0} + a_{1} t + a_{2} t^{2}.\]

Substitute into the differential equation and equate coefficients of like powers:

\[\begin{aligned}6 - 6 a_{2} = 0\\- 6 a_{1} - 2 a_{2} + 14 = 0\\- 6 a_{0} - a_{1} + 2 a_{2} - 6 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a_{0}=-1,\quad a_{1}=2,\quad a_{2}=1\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=t^{2} + 2 t - 1.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{3 t} + C_{2} e^{- 2 t} + t^{2} + 2 t - 1.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=3 C_{1} e^{3 t} - 2 C_{2} e^{- 2 t} + 2 t + 2.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} + C_{2} = 3\\3 C_{1} - 2 C_{2} = -1\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=1,\qquad C_2=2.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=t^{2} + 2 t + e^{3 t} - 1 + 2 e^{- 2 t}.\]

(b)

The complementary terms are \(C_1e^{3t}+C_2e^{-2t}\). At zero, \(C_1+C_2=3\). Removing growth requires \(C_1=0\), so \(C_2=3\). Hence \(v=-2(3)+2=-4\).

\[a_{0}=1,\quad a_{1}=-6,\quad a_{2}=3\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=3 t^{2} - 6 t + 1.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- t} \cos{\left(\frac{\sqrt{6} t}{3} \right)} + C_{2} e^{- t} \sin{\left(\frac{\sqrt{6} t}{3} \right)} + 3 t^{2} - 6 t + 1.\]

original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +3\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +4\,y=12 t^{2} + 26 t + 8\]
(a)[6]

Find the general solution, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[2]

Deduce the limit of \(y^{\prime\prime}\) as \(t\to\infty\).

(a)

(b)

\[y^{\prime\prime}\longrightarrow6.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation is

\[m^{2} + 3 m + 4=0,\qquad m=- \frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}i.\]

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a_{0} + a_{1} t + a_{2} t^{2}.\]

Substitute into the differential equation and equate coefficients of like powers:

\[\begin{aligned}4 a_{2} - 12 = 0\\4 a_{1} + 6 a_{2} - 26 = 0\\4 a_{0} + 3 a_{1} + 2 a_{2} - 8 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a_{0}=-1,\quad a_{1}=2,\quad a_{2}=3\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=3 t^{2} + 2 t - 1.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \cos{\left(\frac{\sqrt{7} t}{2} \right)} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \sin{\left(\frac{\sqrt{7} t}{2} \right)} + 3 t^{2} + 2 t - 1.\]

original.stem_html:

The function \(y\) satisfies

(a)[8]

Find the solution satisfying these conditions, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[3]

Find the exact value of \(x\) where \(y=0\), and justify that it is unique.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

(b)

original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=3 e^{\frac{2 x}{3}} - 2 - 3 e^{- \frac{2 x}{3}}\]

(b)

\[x=\frac32\ln\!\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{10}}3\right).\]

(a)

The auxiliary equation has two distinct real roots:

\[\left(3 m - 2\right) \left(3 m + 2\right)=0,\qquad m=\frac{2}{3},\ - \frac{2}{3}.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{\frac{2 x}{3}} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{2 x}{3}}.\]

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a_{0}.\]

Substitute into the differential equation and equate coefficients of like powers:

\[\begin{aligned}- 4 a_{0} - 8 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a_{0}=-2\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=-2.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{\frac{2 x}{3}} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{2 x}{3}} - 2.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=\frac{2 C_{1} e^{\frac{2 x}{3}}}{3} - \frac{2 C_{2} e^{- \frac{2 x}{3}}}{3}.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} + C_{2} = 0\\\frac{2 C_{1}}{3} - \frac{2 C_{2}}{3} = 4\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=3,\qquad C_2=-3.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=3 e^{\frac{2 x}{3}} - 2 - 3 e^{- \frac{2 x}{3}}.\]

original.title: Two initial conditions on a forced damped system
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[2\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +6\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +5\,y=5 t^{2} + 22 t + 31\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=0\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=0\).
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[2\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +6\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +5\,y=5 t^{2} + 22 t + 31\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=0\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=0\).

(a)[10]

Find the solution satisfying these conditions, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=t^{2} + 2 t + 3 - 13 e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \sin{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)} - 3 e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \cos{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation is

\[2 m^{2} + 6 m + 5=0,\qquad m=- \frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{1}{2}i.\]

Use the real complementary function formed from the conjugate roots.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \cos{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \sin{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}.\]

For a polynomial particular integral, try

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a_{0} + a_{1} t + a_{2} t^{2}.\]

Substitute into the differential equation and equate coefficients of like powers:

\[\begin{aligned}5 a_{2} - 5 = 0\\5 a_{1} + 12 a_{2} - 22 = 0\\5 a_{0} + 6 a_{1} + 4 a_{2} - 31 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a_{0}=3,\quad a_{1}=2,\quad a_{2}=1\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=t^{2} + 2 t + 3.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \cos{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \sin{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)} + t^{2} + 2 t + 3.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- \frac{C_{1} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \sin{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}}{2} - \frac{3 C_{1} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \cos{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}}{2} - \frac{3 C_{2} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \sin{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}}{2} + \frac{C_{2} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \cos{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}}{2} + 2 t + 2.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = -3\\- \frac{3 C_{1}}{2} + \frac{C_{2}}{2} = -2\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=-3,\qquad C_2=-13.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=t^{2} + 2 t + 3 - 13 e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \sin{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)} - 3 e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} \cos{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}.\]

original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +5\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +6\,y=18 t + 3\]
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +5\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +6\,y=18 t + 3\]
(a)[6]

Find the general solution, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[1]

State a large-\(t\) approximation.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

(b)

Examine the complementary function as well as the particular integral.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 2 t} + C_{2} e^{- 3 t} + 3 t - 2\]

(b)

\[y\approx3t-2.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation has two distinct real roots:

\[\left(m + 2\right) \left(m + 3\right)=0,\qquad m=-2,\ -3.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- 2 t} + C_{2} e^{- 3 t}.\]

For a polynomial particular integral, try

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a_{0} + a_{1} t.\]

Substitute into the differential equation and equate coefficients of like powers:

\[\begin{aligned}6 a_{1} - 18 = 0\\6 a_{0} + 5 a_{1} - 3 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a_{0}=-2,\quad a_{1}=3\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=3 t - 2.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 2 t} + C_{2} e^{- 3 t} + 3 t - 2.\]

(b)

The complementary terms are multiples of \(e^{-2t}\) and \(e^{-3t}\), so they decay.

original.title: An exponential input with a repeated decay rate
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[9\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +6\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +y=4 e^{- t}\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=-1\).
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[9\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +6\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +y=4 e^{- t}\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=-1\).

(a)[9]

Find the solution satisfying these conditions, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[1]

State \(\lim_{t\to\infty}y\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

(b)

Examine the complementary function as well as the particular integral.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\frac{t e^{- \frac{t}{3}}}{3} + e^{- t} + e^{- \frac{t}{3}}\]

(b)

\[\lim_{t\to\infty}y=0.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation has a repeated real root:

\[\left(3 m + 1\right)^{2}=0,\qquad m=- \frac{1}{3}.\]

The repeated root requires the extra linear factor, not two copies of the same exponential.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- \frac{t}{3}} + C_{2} t e^{- \frac{t}{3}}.\]

Try \(y_{\mathrm{PI}}=K e^{- t}\). Substitution gives

\[4 K=4,\qquad K=1.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=e^{- t}.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- \frac{t}{3}} + C_{2} t e^{- \frac{t}{3}} + e^{- t}.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- \frac{C_{1} e^{- \frac{t}{3}}}{3} - \frac{C_{2} t e^{- \frac{t}{3}}}{3} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{t}{3}} - e^{- t}.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = 1\\- \frac{C_{1}}{3} + C_{2} = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=1,\qquad C_2=\frac{1}{3}.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=\frac{t e^{- \frac{t}{3}}}{3} + e^{- t} + e^{- \frac{t}{3}}.\]

(b)

Both exponential rates are negative, and \(te^{-t/3}\) also tends to zero.

original.title: A repeated root driven by two harmonics
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[4\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +12\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +9\,y=46 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 9 \cos{\left(t \right)}\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=0\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=0\).
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[4\,\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +12\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +9\,y=46 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 9 \cos{\left(t \right)}\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=0\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=0\).

(a)[9]

Find the solution satisfying these conditions, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[1]

State a periodic approximation for large positive \(t\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

(b)

Examine the complementary function as well as the particular integral.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\frac{5 t e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}}}{2} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 3 \cos{\left(t \right)} + 3 e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}}\]

(b)

\[y\approx2\sin t-3\cos t.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation has a repeated real root:

\[\left(2 m + 3\right)^{2}=0,\qquad m=- \frac{3}{2}.\]

The repeated root requires the extra linear factor, not two copies of the same exponential.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} + C_{2} t e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}}.\]

Try a particular integral containing both sine and cosine:

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a \cos{\left(t \right)} + b \sin{\left(t \right)}.\]

Equating cosine and sine coefficients gives

\[\begin{aligned}5 a + 12 b - 9 = 0\\- 12 a + 5 b - 46 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a=-3,\qquad b=2.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} + C_{2} t e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- \frac{3 C_{1} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}}}{2} - \frac{3 C_{2} t e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}}}{2} + C_{2} e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}} + 3 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = 3\\- \frac{3 C_{1}}{2} + C_{2} = -2\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=3,\qquad C_2=\frac{5}{2}.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=\frac{5 t e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}}}{2} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 3 \cos{\left(t \right)} + 3 e^{- \frac{3 t}{2}}.\]

(b)

The complementary function \((C_1+C_2t)e^{-3t/2}\) tends to zero.

original.title: Amplitude and phase after the transient has decayed
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +2\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +5\,y=17 \sin{\left(2 t \right)}\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=0\).
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +2\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +5\,y=17 \sin{\left(2 t \right)}\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=0\).

(a)[10]

Find the solution satisfying these conditions, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[3]

Show that, for any initial conditions and large positive \(t\), the solution is approximately \(R\sin(2t-\phi)\). Find exact \(R\) and \(\tan\phi\), with \(0\lt \phi\lt \pi/2\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

(b)

The minus sign before the cosine determines the sign of the phase shift.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=\sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 4 \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 e^{- t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 6 e^{- t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\]

(b)

\[R=\sqrt{17},\qquad \tan\phi=4.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation is

\[m^{2} + 2 m + 5=0,\qquad m=-1\pm 2i.\]

Use the real complementary function formed from the conjugate roots.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

Try a particular integral containing both sine and cosine:

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + b \sin{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

Equating cosine and sine coefficients gives

\[\begin{aligned}a + 4 b = 0\\- 4 a + b - 17 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a=-4,\qquad b=1.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=\sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 4 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 4 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- 2 C_{1} e^{- t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - C_{1} e^{- t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} - C_{2} e^{- t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 C_{2} e^{- t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + 8 \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = 6\\- C_{1} + 2 C_{2} = -2\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=6,\qquad C_2=2.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=\sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 4 \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 e^{- t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 6 e^{- t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

(b)

The complementary function tends to zero because of \(e^{-t}\). Expand the desired form:

\[R\sin(2t-\phi)=R\cos\phi\sin2t-R\sin\phi\cos2t.\]

Matching gives \(R\cos\phi=1\) and \(R\sin\phi=4\). Thus \(R=\sqrt{17}\) and the specified first-quadrant phase has \(\tan\phi=4\).

\[\begin{aligned}12 a + 16 b = 0\\- 16 a + 12 b - 100 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a=-4,\qquad b=3.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=3 \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 4 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

original.title: Why an oscillatory particular integral may not dominate
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} -4\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +4\,y=10 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 5 \cos{\left(t \right)}\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=3\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=-1\).
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} -4\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +4\,y=10 \sin{\left(t \right)} - 5 \cos{\left(t \right)}\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=3\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=-1\).

(a)[9]

Find the solution satisfying these conditions, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[2]

Is the particular integral a valid large-\(t\) approximation for this initial-value problem? Explain.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

(b)

Examine the complementary function as well as the particular integral.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=- 7 t e^{2 t} + 2 e^{2 t} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}\]

(b)

No.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation has a repeated real root:

\[\left(m - 2\right)^{2}=0,\qquad m=2.\]

The repeated root requires the extra linear factor, not two copies of the same exponential.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{2 t} + C_{2} t e^{2 t}.\]

Try a particular integral containing both sine and cosine:

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a \cos{\left(t \right)} + b \sin{\left(t \right)}.\]

Equating cosine and sine coefficients gives

\[\begin{aligned}3 a - 4 b + 5 = 0\\4 a + 3 b - 10 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a=1,\qquad b=2.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=2 \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{2 t} + C_{2} t e^{2 t} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=2 C_{1} e^{2 t} + 2 C_{2} t e^{2 t} + C_{2} e^{2 t} - \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = 2\\2 C_{1} + C_{2} = -3\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=2,\qquad C_2=-7.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=- 7 t e^{2 t} + 2 e^{2 t} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

(b)

The complementary part is \((2-7t)e^{2t}\), which grows in magnitude and tends to negative infinity. The bounded periodic particular integral does not dominate the solution.

original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} -3\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} -4\,y=4 \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 22 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=\frac{5}{2}\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=\frac{1}{2}\).
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} -3\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} -4\,y=4 \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 22 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\]

At \(t=0\), \(y=\frac{5}{2}\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t}=\frac{1}{2}\).

(a)[11]

Find the solution satisfying these conditions, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=- \frac{e^{4 t}}{5} + \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + \frac{7 e^{- t}}{10}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation has two distinct real roots:

\[\left(m - 4\right) \left(m + 1\right)=0,\qquad m=4,\ -1.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{4 t} + C_{2} e^{- t}.\]

Try a particular integral containing both sine and cosine:

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + b \sin{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

Equating cosine and sine coefficients gives

\[\begin{aligned}- 8 a - 6 b + 22 = 0\\6 a - 8 b - 4 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a=2,\qquad b=1.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=\sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{4 t} + C_{2} e^{- t} + \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=4 C_{1} e^{4 t} - C_{2} e^{- t} - 4 \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} + C_{2} = \frac{1}{2}\\4 C_{1} - C_{2} = - \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=- \frac{1}{5},\qquad C_2=\frac{7}{10}.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=- \frac{e^{4 t}}{5} + \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + \frac{7 e^{- t}}{10}.\]

original.question_html:

original.title: A complete forced-response investigation
original.stem_html:
For \(t\ge0\), the response \(y\) satisfies

\[y^{\prime\prime}+6y^\prime+13y=90\cos t.\]
original.question_html:
For \(t\ge0\), the response \(y\) satisfies

\[y^{\prime\prime}+6y^\prime+13y=90\cos t.\]
(a)[6]

Find the general solution.

(b)[4]

Find the solution with \(y(0)=4\) and \(y^\prime(0)=0\).

(c)[4]

Show that every solution is asymptotic, in the sense of a vanishing difference, to \(R\cos(t-\phi)\). Determine \(R\) and \(\phi\) exactly, with \(0\lt \phi\lt \pi/2\). State whether \(y\) has a limit.
original.hint_html:
(a)

A sine term is needed in the particular integral even though the input is a cosine.

(b)

Use the complete general solution when applying initial conditions.

(c)

For a cosine phase shift the cosine coefficient is \(R\cos\phi\); do not swap sine and cosine.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 3 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)}\]

(b)

\[y=3 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)} - \frac{9 e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} - 2 e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\]

(c)

\[R=3\sqrt5,\qquad \phi=\tan^{-1}\!\frac12.\]

There is no pointwise limit.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation is

\[m^{2} + 6 m + 13=0,\qquad m=-3\pm 2i.\]

Use the real complementary function formed from the conjugate roots.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

Try a particular integral containing both sine and cosine:

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a \cos{\left(t \right)} + b \sin{\left(t \right)}.\]

Equating cosine and sine coefficients gives

\[\begin{aligned}12 a + 6 b - 90 = 0\\- 6 a + 12 b = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a=6,\qquad b=3.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=3 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

Add the complementary function and particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 3 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)}\]

(b)

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- 2 C_{1} e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 3 C_{1} e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} - 3 C_{2} e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 C_{2} e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} - 6 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = -2\\- 3 C_{1} + 2 C_{2} = -3\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=-2,\qquad C_2=- \frac{9}{2}.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=3 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 6 \cos{\left(t \right)} - \frac{9 e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} - 2 e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

(c)

The complementary function decays as \(e^{-3t}\). Since \(R\cos(t-\phi)=R\cos\phi\cos t+R\sin\phi\sin t\), coefficient comparison gives \(R\cos\phi=6\) and \(R\sin\phi=3\). Thus \(R=3\sqrt5\) and \(\tan\phi=1/2\). Along \(t=2n\pi\) the solution tends to 6, but along \(t=(2n+1)\pi\) it tends to \(-6\). Therefore it does not converge to a single value.

\[y^\prime=- 2 C_{1} e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 3 C_{1} e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} - 3 C_{2} e^{- 3 t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + 2 C_{2} e^{- 3 t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} - 6 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 3 \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = -2\\- 3 C_{1} + 2 C_{2} = -3\end{aligned}\]

original.title: Separating general, particular and long-term solutions
original.stem_html:
The equation is

\[y^{\prime\prime}+4y^\prime+5y=8\sin t.\]
original.question_html:
The equation is

\[y^{\prime\prime}+4y^\prime+5y=8\sin t.\]
(a)[6]

Find the general solution.

(b)[3]

Find the solution with \(y(0)=3\) and \(y^\prime(0)=2\).

(c)[2]

Give a periodic approximation valid for large positive \(t\) and explain why it is independent of the initial conditions.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Do not apply initial conditions before writing the two-constant general solution.

(b)

Differentiate the complementary exponential factor as well as the trigonometric factors.

(c)

Locate the constants introduced by the initial data.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 2 t} \cos{\left(t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}\]

(b)

\[y=\sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)} + 9 e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(t \right)} + 4 e^{- 2 t} \cos{\left(t \right)}\]

(c)

\[y\approx\sin t-\cos t.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation is

\[m^{2} + 4 m + 5=0,\qquad m=-2\pm 1i.\]

Use the real complementary function formed from the conjugate roots.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- 2 t} \cos{\left(t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(t \right)}.\]

Try a particular integral containing both sine and cosine:

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a \cos{\left(t \right)} + b \sin{\left(t \right)}.\]

Equating cosine and sine coefficients gives

\[\begin{aligned}4 a + 4 b = 0\\- 4 a + 4 b - 8 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a=-1,\qquad b=1.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=\sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]
\[y=C_{1} e^{- 2 t} \cos{\left(t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)}\]

(b)

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- C_{1} e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(t \right)} - 2 C_{1} e^{- 2 t} \cos{\left(t \right)} - 2 C_{2} e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(t \right)} + C_{2} e^{- 2 t} \cos{\left(t \right)} + \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = 4\\- 2 C_{1} + C_{2} = 1\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=4,\qquad C_2=9.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=\sin{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(t \right)} + 9 e^{- 2 t} \sin{\left(t \right)} + 4 e^{- 2 t} \cos{\left(t \right)}.\]

(c)

All initial-condition dependence is in \(e^{-2t}(C_1\cos t+C_2\sin t)\). This tends to zero for every fixed \(C_1,C_2\).

original.title: A periodic asymptote is not a limit
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +2\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +y=25 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\]
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +2\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +y=25 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\]
(a)[6]

Find the general solution, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[2]

Describe the behaviour as \(t\to\infty\), making clear whether a limit exists.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

(b)

Examine the complementary function as well as the particular integral.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=C_{1} e^{- t} + C_{2} t e^{- t} + 4 \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 3 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\]

(b)

The difference from \(4\sin2t-3\cos2t\) tends to zero, but \(y\) has no limit.
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation has a repeated real root:

\[\left(m + 1\right)^{2}=0,\qquad m=-1.\]

The repeated root requires the extra linear factor, not two copies of the same exponential.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- t} + C_{2} t e^{- t}.\]

Try a particular integral containing both sine and cosine:

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a \cos{\left(2 t \right)} + b \sin{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

Equating cosine and sine coefficients gives

\[\begin{aligned}- 3 a + 4 b - 25 = 0\\- 4 a - 3 b = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a=-3,\qquad b=4.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=4 \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 3 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- t} + C_{2} t e^{- t} + 4 \sin{\left(2 t \right)} - 3 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}.\]

(b)

The transient \((C_1+C_2t)e^{-t}\) decays. Along \(t=n\pi\) the limiting values are \(-3\), while along \(t=n\pi+\pi/2\) they are 3. This rules out convergence.

original.title: Choosing the phase in the correct quadrant
original.stem_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +6\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +8\,y=56 \sin{\left(3 t \right)} - 33 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\]
original.question_html:
The function \(y\) satisfies

\[\frac{\mathrm d^2 y}{\mathrm d t^2} +6\,\frac{\mathrm d y}{\mathrm d t} +8\,y=56 \sin{\left(3 t \right)} - 33 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\]
(a)[6]

Find the general solution, showing the complementary function and a particular integral separately.

(b)[3]

For large positive \(t\), express the solution approximately as \(R\sin(3t+\phi)\), with \(R\gt 0\) and \(0\lt \phi\lt 2\pi\). Give \(R\) and \(\phi\) to 2 decimal places.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Solve the auxiliary equation first. Determine the particular integral independently; apply initial conditions only after adding the two pieces.

(b)

Both coefficients are negative; use their signs as well as their ratio.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 2 t} + C_{2} e^{- 4 t} - 2 \sin{\left(3 t \right)} - 3 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}\]

(b)

\[R=\sqrt{13}\approx3.61,\qquad \phi=\pi+\tan^{-1}\!\frac32\approx4.12.\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

The auxiliary equation has two distinct real roots:

\[\left(m + 2\right) \left(m + 4\right)=0,\qquad m=-2,\ -4.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- 2 t} + C_{2} e^{- 4 t}.\]

Try a particular integral containing both sine and cosine:

\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=a \cos{\left(3 t \right)} + b \sin{\left(3 t \right)}.\]

Equating cosine and sine coefficients gives

\[\begin{aligned}- a + 18 b + 33 = 0\\- 18 a - b - 56 = 0\end{aligned}\]
\[a=-3,\qquad b=-2.\]
\[y_{\mathrm{PI}}=- 2 \sin{\left(3 t \right)} - 3 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}.\]

The general solution is the sum of the complementary function and the particular integral:

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 2 t} + C_{2} e^{- 4 t} - 2 \sin{\left(3 t \right)} - 3 \cos{\left(3 t \right)}.\]

(b)

The complementary terms decay. Comparing \(R\cos\phi=-2\) and \(R\sin\phi=-3\) puts \(\phi\) in quadrant III. Therefore \(R=\sqrt{13}\) and \(\phi=\pi+\tan^{-1}(3/2)\). Giving only \(\tan^{-1}(3/2)\) would select the wrong quadrant.

original.title: A resonant exponential with a supplied trial form
original.stem_html:
Consider

\[y^{\prime\prime}-y^\prime-6y=5e^{-2x}.\]
original.question_html:
Consider

\[y^{\prime\prime}-y^\prime-6y=5e^{-2x}.\]
(a)[3]

Find \(K\) such that \(Kxe^{-2x}\) is a particular integral.

(b)[7]

Hence find the solution satisfying \(y(0)=3\) and \(y^\prime(0)=-2\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The extra factor \(x\) is essential because \(e^{-2x}\) already occurs in the complementary function.

(b)

Add the resonant particular integral before applying both initial conditions.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[K=-1.\]

(b)

\[y=- x e^{- 2 x} + e^{3 x} + 2 e^{- 2 x}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

For \(y_p=Kxe^{-2x}\),

original.title: A repeated resonant root
original.stem_html:
Consider

\[y^{\prime\prime}+4y^\prime+4y=6e^{-2x}.\]
original.question_html:
Consider

\[y^{\prime\prime}+4y^\prime+4y=6e^{-2x}.\]
(a)[3]

Find \(K\) such that \(Kx^2e^{-2x}\) is a particular integral.

(b)[3]

Hence find the general solution.

(c)[5]

Find the solution with \(y(0)=2\) and \(y^\prime(0)=1\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Both \(e^{-2x}\) and \(xe^{-2x}\) already occur in the complementary function.

(b)

Use the repeated-root complementary function.

(c)

The derivative of \(e^{-2x}\) contributes to both initial equations.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\[K=3.\]

(b)

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 2 x} + C_{2} x e^{- 2 x} + 3 x^{2} e^{- 2 x}\]

(c)

\[y=3 x^{2} e^{- 2 x} + 5 x e^{- 2 x} + 2 e^{- 2 x}\]
original.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the supplied form twice:

\[y_p^\prime=K(2x-2x^2)e^{-2x},\qquad y_p^{\prime\prime}=K(2-8x+4x^2)e^{-2x}.\]

The left side simplifies to \(2Ke^{-2x}\), so \(2K=6\).

(b)

The auxiliary equation has a repeated real root:

\[\left(m + 2\right)^{2}=0,\qquad m=-2.\]

The repeated root requires the extra linear factor, not two copies of the same exponential.

\[y_{\mathrm{CF}}=C_{1} e^{- 2 x} + C_{2} x e^{- 2 x}.\]

Add the particular integral from part (a):

\[y=C_{1} e^{- 2 x} + C_{2} x e^{- 2 x} + 3 x^{2} e^{- 2 x}\]

(c)

Differentiate the general solution before applying the derivative condition:

\[y^\prime=- 2 C_{1} e^{- 2 x} - 2 C_{2} x e^{- 2 x} + C_{2} e^{- 2 x} - 6 x^{2} e^{- 2 x} + 6 x e^{- 2 x}.\]

At the stated initial point, the two conditions give

\[\begin{aligned}C_{1} = 2\\- 2 C_{1} + C_{2} = 1\end{aligned}\]
\[C_1=2,\qquad C_2=5.\]

Substituting these constants gives

\[y=3 x^{2} e^{- 2 x} + 5 x e^{- 2 x} + 2 e^{- 2 x}.\]
